links.note: Classifying your own town, village or city by landform type applies this concept's three broad categories, mountains, plateaus and plains, to the reader's own surroundings. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.

The trip from Chhota Nagpur to Prayagraj and Almora is this concept's own opening journey - travelling by road from Jharkhand to Uttar Pradesh and on to Uttarakhand, encountering three major landforms on the way - and the question explicitly sends the reader back to it.

Listing famous pilgrimage spots in India with the landforms they are found in is verbatim one of the chapter's closing questions in this concept, and it ranges across mountains, plateaus and plains rather than any single section.

The eight matching pairs, from Mount Everest and climbing to the plateau and the roof of the world, are the closing match exercise this concept describes; the pairs are drawn from every section of the chapter.
A landform defined as a physical feature on the surface of our planet Earth - this concept's definition, which the chapter gives only after the journey has been imagined.
Landforms divided broadly into three categories, mountains, plateaus and plains - stated in this concept.
Altitude as height above mean sea level - this is the concept where altitude does its work in the chapter, with snow melting every summer at lower altitudes and never melting at high altitudes.
Snow melting every summer at lower altitudes and turning into water that feeds rivers - this concept's opening sentence. Already linked and correct.
Precipitation defined as water from the atmosphere reaching the ground in any form, with rain, snow and hail the commonest - this concept's gloss. Already linked and correct.

The Himalayas as the mountain range in Asia holding the world's highest peaks - this concept opens on the Himalayas in Asia, the Alps in Europe and the Andes in South America, which are exactly the distractors.
Kanchenjunga between Nepal and Sikkim - this concept names it as one of the two highest peaks of the Himalayan range, beside Everest.
Mount Kilimanjaro in eastern Africa, an isolated mountain that is not part of any range - this concept's own description of it.
Anamudi in Kerala, also known as Anai Peak, the highest mountain in South India - the last of the six peaks this concept shows side by side.
Montane forest with conifer trees such as pines, firs, spruce and deodar - this concept's opening sentence.
At higher altitudes the trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen - this concept's sentence, immediately after the montane forest.

The risk of sudden landslides as a natural challenge of mountain life - landslide is glossed in this concept as the sudden collapse of a mass of earth or rock from a mountainside, among the hazards listed after the two climbers.
Chomolungma, the Tibetan name for Everest meaning Mother Goddess of the World - this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box on sacred mountains, where Sagarmatha is the Nepali name given as the distractor.
The Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha in the Chhota Nagpur Plateau - one of the four waterfalls this concept names.
Floodplains formed as rivers from mountain ranges carry sediments to the plains and deposit them - this concept's definition. Already linked and correct.
Plains ideal for growing crops because their soil is fertile - this concept explains that the deposited sediments make the soil very fertile, which is why agriculture is the major occupation there.
Irrigation contributing to the depletion of groundwater is named in this concept as the challenge for the future of agriculture in the Ganga plain.
Confluence as the meeting point of rivers - this concept is where a river's source and its confluence with one or two other rivers are held sacred, with festivals and rituals conducted there.
The gentle slope of plains making river navigation easy - this concept's closing point, with stretches along the Ganga where people still prefer boats.
The five tinais of ancient Tamil Sangam poetry - this concept lists all five and is the only one that mentions them.
Kurinji as the mountainous tinai whose occupation is hunting and gathering - the first row of this concept's table of five landscapes.
Mountains against hills - this concept defines hills as other highlands with a lower height, less steep slopes and rounded tops, which is the distinction the item turns on.
Pairing the Andes with South America - this concept's opening sentence gives the Himalayas in Asia, the Alps in Europe and the Andes in South America, and the Aravalli appears here too.
Growing crops on a steep mountainside by cutting steps into the slope is terrace farming, which this concept defines and explains as a response to rugged terrain.
Plateaus called storehouses of minerals, with mining a major activity - this concept's own phrase and reasoning. Already linked and correct.
The Tibetan Plateau nicknamed the Roof of the World because of its average altitude of 4,500 m - this concept's sentence. Already linked and correct.
Ruling out urban cities as a major landform is decided against this concept's three categories, mountains, plateaus and plains, which are the other three options.
Fertile floodplain soil from deposited fine sediments - this concept names particles of rock, sand and silt called sediments as what the rivers carry and deposit. Already linked and correct.
Matching Neydal with coastal regions against the kurinji, mullai and marudam distractors is read straight off this concept's table of the five tinais.

A region with very little precipitation and sparse specially adapted vegetation is a desert - this concept defines deserts as large dry expanses with very little precipitation whose flora and fauna are unique.
Young mountains like the Himalayas having tall and sharp peaks - this concept reads age off shape, contrasting them with the shorter, rounded Aravalli Range.

The one visible statement, that plains generally have fertile soil, is judged against this concept's floodplains, where deposited sediments make the soil very fertile. The item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The first civilisations developing around rivers in fertile plains thousands of years ago is this concept's opening sentence, and water plus fertile land is the reason it gives.
Palai as the arid desert-like tinai whose occupation is journeying and fighting - the last row of this concept's table. Already linked and correct.

Lichen as a plant-like organism clinging to rocks - lichen appears in this concept where, at higher altitudes, the trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen, with moss as the competing option from the same phrase.
Mont Blanc as the highest of the Alps is the one correct pair, and every mountain in the four options - Everest, Anamudi, Kilimanjaro, Mont Blanc - comes from this concept's six peaks.

Picking out ease of transportation as the one thing that is not a mountain challenge is decided against this concept's hazard list - flash flood, landslide, avalanche and cloudburst, each glossed there.

Terrain as a stretch of land seen through its physical features - the word is introduced in this concept, where the mountain terrain being rugged with steep slopes is the reason regular farming is limited to some valleys.
A physical feature on the surface of our planet Earth is a landform - this concept's definition, stated in those words.
The three broad categories of landforms, mountains, plateaus and plains - listed in this concept.
Altitude as the height of a point above sea level - this concept is where the chapter uses altitude as a working variable, lower altitudes against high altitudes deciding whether snow melts.
Highlands with a lower height, less steep slopes and rounded tops are called hills - this concept's sentence, word for word.
Naming a major mountain range in Asia - this concept opens on the Himalayas in Asia among the world's mountain ranges.
Mount Everest as the world's highest peak - this concept is the six-peaks comparison where Everest, between Tibet and Nepal, heads the list.
Bachendri Pal as the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest, in 1984 - this concept introduces her and Arunima Sinha before the mountain hazards are named.
Flash flood glossed as a sudden local flood often caused by a cloudburst - the vocabulary supplied in this concept beside landslide, avalanche and cloudburst.
About 40 crore people, more than a fourth of India's population, living in the Ganga plain - this concept's figure. Already linked and correct.
Rice among the food crops of the Gangetic plain - this concept lists rice, wheat, maize, barley and millets as the food crops and cotton, jute and hemp as the fibre crops.
